raw_response:
I'm 58 this year, and I've been farming these 9.5 mu for 35 years since I married into this village. I finished middle school, so I can read the extension pamphlets they hand out at the township meetings and I understand what the young technician says, but honestly I trust my own eyes more than what someone reads from a book. My husband is 61 and his back isn't what it used to be, so I handle most of the day-to-day work and decisions now. There are three of us in the household — my husband, me, and our son who works in a factory in Handan and sends some money home. But I don't like to count on that. This farm has to pay for itself.

I keep three crops because I've learned the hard way that putting all your land in one basket is dangerous. Five years ago when the cotton bollworm was bad and the price dropped, if I hadn't had my cauliflower and stevia to sell, we would have eaten into our savings. So this year it's the same as last year: 5 mu of cotton, 2.5 mu of spring cauliflower, and 2 mu of stevia that I planted three years ago and is still producing well.

My cauliflower went in the ground in early March — I bought seedlings from Old Wang at the village market. Right now the heads are starting to form, so I topdressed with urea last week. I expect to harvest in late May or early June. I give it about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as a base before transplanting, and then 15 kg of urea per mu when the curd starts forming. I irrigate four times because cauliflower needs steady moisture to form good heads, but every time I start the pump the electricity meter spins, so I don't waste water.

For cotton, I'm planting right now in mid-to-late April. I buy hybrid seed every year from the county supply store — 65 yuan per mu. I know some people save their own seed but I tried that about ten years ago and the plants were weak and the yield was poor. Never again. For fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer in the rows before planting, and then topdress with urea at flowering in early July. The extension fellow says I should use 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, but last year I tried 18 and spent more money without seeing much difference from 15 kg. At around 4 yuan per kilo for urea, that extra 3 kg per mu across 5 mu is 60 yuan that I'd rather keep in my pocket. Cotton needs water at critical times, so I'll irrigate three times — at planting, flowering, and boll filling.

The stevia is easy money at this point. It comes back from the roots every spring. I just cultivate between the rows, put down about 30 kg of compound fertilizer per mu in April, and cut the leaves twice — once in mid-July and again in mid-September. The buyer from the processing plant drives right to the village, so I don't have to haul it far. It barely needs any pesticide, which saves me money and effort.

For labor, my husband helps with plowing and carrying heavy bags, but I handle the spraying, fertilizing, irrigation, and day-to-day watching. I hire help for the busy times — about six days for cotton picking in October because I can't pick 5 mu by myself before the weather turns, two days for cauliflower transplanting and harvest, and one day for the second stevia cutting. Hiring costs 150 yuan per day now, which hurts, but missing the harvest window hurts more.

My total input costs this year will be about 5,100 yuan. That's a big chunk of cash for a household like ours, but the cauliflower will bring in money first in June, then stevia in July and September, and cotton in October. I keep about 2,000 yuan in reserve for emergencies — three years ago my husband needed medicine and the hospital wanted payment upfront. So I'm not pushing for maximum fertilizer or maximum yield. I know what my land can do, and I'd rather sleep soundly knowing I have money in the jar than gamble on an extra 50 kg of urea.
